Hoaxes: The War of the Worlds (1938 radio drama)

first.title: Floods That Were Not Water
first.note: In 1814 a wave of beer broke through a London brewery wall, and afterwards the brewery got a tax refund on the beer.

moments.text: Ishai finds a seat as Dr. Sasson opens the first lecture of Strange But True.

lines.say: Sit anywhere, Ishai. Welcome to Strange But True. Everything in this course really happened, and that's the problem.
Sorry I'm late. The bus stopped at every stop. I think it stopped at a few that aren't stops.
You're on time. Look at the board. Every lecture has a title, and the next one is always written underneath.
Today: Floods That Were Not Water. Two cities, about a hundred years apart, two tanks, and one very old question.
What's the question?
When a tank bursts and people die, who pays? Keep that in your notebook. We'll come back to it at the end.
Is that going to be on the test?
There's no test. There's one question at the end of each lecture, and I will look at you while I ask it.
We start in London, October 1814. The Horse Shoe Brewery, where Tottenham Court Road meets Oxford Street.
It belongs to Meux and Company, one of the two biggest brewers in the city. They brew one thing only: porter.
And big brewers like big vats. Size is how you show the rest of London who you are.
Henry Meux's father built the largest vat in London. So Henry builds a giant of his own, and straps it with iron.
So this is basically two men comparing barrels.
That is the most accurate summary of the Industrial Revolution I've heard this year.

commentary.say: A lecture hall. He has entered a building with no snacks on purpose.

moments.text: Dr. Sasson tells the class about the clerk and the slipped iron band.

lines.say: Behind the brewery lies New Street, a dead end in the St Giles rookery. Eight acres of slum, many of them Irish families.
Keep that picture in mind: the richest brewers in the city on one side of a wall, the poorest families on the other.
Now meet George Crick, storehouse clerk. Around four thirty on the seventeenth, he sees a problem on one of the vats.
An iron band has slipped. Each band weighs about 320 kilos. The vat is 6.7 metres tall and filled almost to the top.
So he tells someone.
He does! He tells his supervisor. The supervisor says no harm will come of it. Bands slip a few times a year.
Crick is told to write a note to Mr Young, a partner, so it can be fixed later. So he goes and writes the note.
Oh no.
An hour later he's standing about nine metres from the vat, with the note in his hand.
The vat bursts with no warning. The blast knocks the stopcock off a neighbouring vat, and that one empties too.
With the note still in his hand?
With the note in his hand. If this course teaches you one thing, let it be this: paperwork has never stopped a flood.
Nobody agrees how much beer got out. The sources say anywhere from 580,000 to almost one and a half million litres.

commentary.say: A man wrote a note. History remembers the note.

moments.text: The room goes quiet as Dr. Sasson describes New Street.

lines.say: The rear wall of the brewery was 7.6 metres high and two and a half bricks thick. The beer went through it.
Bricks landed on roofs in Great Russell Street. Then a wave about 4.5 metres high went down New Street.
Two houses were destroyed and two more badly damaged. The ground was low and flat, so the beer filled the cellars.
People climbed onto their furniture to keep from drowning. Eight people died.
I'll stop joking for a minute. Five of them were at a wake, in a cellar, mourning a two-year-old boy.
They were at a funeral?
Yes. A four-year-old girl was killed at home, at tea. A fourteen-year-old servant died under the wall, washing pots.
A three-year-old was found in another house. Every worker at the brewery survived.
I remember hearing people ran out with buckets and got drunk in the street.
Good, you've heard the legend. Later stories say hundreds came to collect the beer, and that someone drank himself to death.
A brewing historian, Martyn Cornell, checked the newspapers from the time. No revelry. They describe the crowds as well-behaved.
And those papers disliked the Irish of St Giles. Had anyone misbehaved, he argues, they'd have printed it gladly.
So here's the historian's habit: when a story is too much fun, ask who wrote it down, and when.

moments.text: Dr. Sasson reads out the verdict of the inquest.

lines.say: The inquest met two days later at the St Giles Workhouse. The jury was taken to look at the scene.
George Crick gave evidence. So did the landlord of the Tavistock Arms, the pub where that young servant had worked.
The verdict: the eight had died, and I quote, casually, accidentally and by misfortune.
Meaning what?
Meaning an act of God. And if God did it, nobody owes anybody anything. Meux and Company paid no compensation.
Meanwhile the brewery had lost twenty-three thousand pounds. A huge sum. Now guess who they asked for help.
Their insurance?
Parliament. They petitioned to get back the tax they had paid on the beer. And they got about 7,250 pounds.
Wait. The people who lost their kids got nothing, and the brewery got a refund on the beer that killed them?
Write down exactly what you just said, because you've done history for the first time. It's meant to annoy you.
The public gave money for the funerals. The brewery reopened soon after, and the trade slowly gave up giant wooden vats.
That's the first flood. The law looked at the tank and shrugged. Take a short break. The machine outside eats coins, so be careful.

commentary.say: Refund on the beer. Somebody call Gadi, that is a negotiation.

moments.text: The class comes back in and Dr. Sasson moves on to Boston.

lines.say: Back to your seats. Second flood. Boston, 15 January 1919, the North End. It's about half past twelve in the afternoon.
The Purity Distilling tank stands 15 metres tall and 27 metres across. Inside, around 13,000 tons of molasses.
Molasses like the sweet syrup? That's the flood?
Everyone laughs at this point, and I'd like you to enjoy it now, because you won't later.
Why so much? Molasses makes industrial alcohol. And the owners were reportedly racing a deadline: Prohibition.
The constitutional amendment that banned alcohol was ratified the very next day. You could not write this.
The tank had been leaking since its first filling in 1915. The steel was reportedly half as thick as it should have been.
The job was run by a company treasurer named Arthur Jell. He had no engineering or architectural experience.
And nobody checked him?
He skipped the basic safety tests, and ignored the warning signs. A treasurer. With a budget. And a deadline.
Now the weather. Days of freezing, then it warms up. A ship delivers warmed molasses into the cold stuff in the tank.
It expands. It may be fermenting too, adding gas. The pressure rises against a brittle tank with bad rivets.
Witnesses heard a roar, like an elevated train going by. And they said rivets started shooting out of the sides.

moments.text: Dr. Sasson describes the wave of molasses and the rescue.

lines.say: The wave was maybe 7.6 metres high, moving at about 56 kilometres an hour. Sources disagree, and the plaque says even more.
Nobody can outrun that.
Nobody could. It flooded several blocks, up to about a metre deep. Steel panels hit the girders of the elevated railway.
A streetcar was briefly tipped off its tracks, and a truck was thrown into the harbour. Twenty-one people died.
About 150 were hurt. Here's the cruel part: as it cooled it thickened, and people were trapped in it.
First to arrive were 116 navy cadets from a training ship. They walked straight into it to pull people out.
They searched for four days. Some victims had been swept into the harbour, and were only found months later.
I laughed earlier.
Everyone does. That's why I told you. Now, how do you clean up a city covered in syrup?
Hot water?
Salt water from a fireboat, and sand. It took weeks. The harbour ran brown until summer.
People carried it across the whole city on their shoes. One account said everything a Bostonian touched was sticky.

moments.text: Dr. Sasson puts the two floods side by side and asks the question of the day.

lines.say: So, who pays? This time 119 residents sued the owner, in one of the first class actions in Massachusetts.
The company's defence: anarchists blew up the tank. It took three years of hearings to get an answer.
Did they get away with it? Like in London?
No. The court's auditor found them responsible. They paid 628,000 dollars, about seven thousand for each family who lost someone.
And Boston's rules changed: now a licensed architect and a civil engineer had to oversee work like that.
Look at the two side by side. 1814: act of God, the brewery gets a tax refund. 1919: somebody did this, so pay.
A burst tank and dead neighbours, both times, a century apart. What changed wasn't the engineering. It was the question.
Here is today's question, and yes, I'm looking at you. When something goes wrong, who decides it was nobody's fault?
Whoever's writing the report?
Not bad for a man who lost a coin to a machine. In 2019 they read the twenty-one names aloud. Remember that too.

commentary.say: He answered a question in public. Mark the date.
